div.p: Tumor-to-tumor metastasis is a known but rare occurrence and is characterized as 2 distinct tumor types in same anatomic location. We present a rare case of intracranial tumor-totumor metastasis of esophageal adenocarcinoma into meningioma. Our case emphasizes the rare occurrence of intracranial tumor-to-tumor metastasis and importance of histology and immunohistochemical analysis in distinguishing between metastasis and meningioma, especially when faced with ambiguous demarcation. Awareness of this occurrence is crucial, given that metastases might be the initial indication of an underlying tumor and it can impact the clinical management decisions.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Metastasis of one tumor to another type (tumor-to-tumor metastasis) is a known but rare phenomenon [ 1 ,2 ]. Approximately one-third of advanced solid organ malignancies metastasize to brain [3] . Metastatic intracranial lesions are 10-fold more common than primary brain tumors [4] . Meningioma being the most common intracranial tumor, it frequently harbors the tumor-to-tumor metastasis with breast and lung cancers being the most frequent source of donor tumor [5] . This phenomenon can be seen as first indication of an occult primary malignancy and its recognition critically impacts the evaluation of meningiomas. Relatively similar histo-logical features with a lack of clear demarcation between the metastasis and meningioma may challenge its recognition, especially initially. Our case showcases an unusual presentation of highly advanced esophageal adenocarcinoma metastasizing to intracranial meningioma. underwent biopsy of distal esophageal mass revealing moderate to poorly differentiated esophageal adenocarcinoma. In addition, at the time of biopsy, the patient was found to have liver metastasis. A review of system was limited given the patient's confusion. A family member reported him to be at baseline health status on a previous day. Patient was not reported to take any medications which can contribute towards altered mental status. On examination, he was hemodynamically stable, alert but only oriented to self. He did not exhibit any focal neurological deficits. CT brain without IV contrast revealed a large, poorly defined, noncalcified, hyperdense mass in left temporal lobe with effacement of left lateral ventricle and 4 mm right-sided midline shift ( Fig. 1 A). There was no hyperostosis of left temporal bone adjacent to a large mass ( Fig. 1 B). MRI brain showed a large extra-axial mass, measuring 4.8 × 2.3 × 4.3 cm at the left fronto-temporal convexity. The mass was isointense on T1WI ( Fig. 2 A) and predominantly hypointense on T2WI with mild surrounding vasogenic edema ( Fig. 2 B). The mass showed heterogenous enhancement with a dural tail ( Fig. 2 C). There was no evidence of brain invasion by dominant mass. No other intracranial meningioma was identified. There are multiple additional small enhancing lesions throughout the supra-and infratentorial brain concerning for metastatic disease ( Fig. 3 ). However, no evidence of leptomeningeal carcinomatosis or bony metastasis were present. The patient underwent a left temporal craniectomy for resection attempt of a large, presumed tumor located at the left frontal-temporal convexity.

div.head: Histopathology
div.p: Microscopic examination of our case revealed 2 types of tumors coexisting in the resected lesion, including both meningioma and adenocarcinoma ( Fig. 4 A). The meningioma ex-hibits lobulated and whorled pattern with scattered microcalcification. The individual meningioma tumor cells demonstrate oval enlarged nuclei harboring loose chromatin and frequent nuclear grooves. Mitosis is sparse and rare. No atypical features are seen in the meningioma. Therefore, this meningioma is designated as a conventional meningioma (WHO grade 1). As expected, the meningioma is confirmed with positive SSTR2A (somatostatin receptor 2A) immunohistochemical stain ( Fig. 4 B). Adjacent to the meningioma are metastatic adenocarcinoma, exhibiting glandular pattern, marked hyperchromatic anaplastic nuclei, frequent mitoses, and tumor necrosis. This metastatic adenocarcinoma express CK20 (Cytokeratin 20) and CDX2 (caudal type homeobox 2) ( Figs. 4 C and D), suggesting a likely primary origin from hindgut gastrointestinal tract.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Tumor-to-tumor metastasis is characterized by hematogenous metastatic spread of secondary tumor into the primary recipient mass [1] . In contrast, collision tumors are observed as simultaneous growth of 2 different tumors within same organ and often invading each other [ 1 ,2 ]. These rare phenomena are often used interchangeably in the Literature. Following diagnostic criteria, our case stands out as an instance of esophageal adenocarcinoma metastasizing into meningioma, an occurrence reported only once previously [6] .

Literature reviews suggest an uncommon occurrence of these tumor types with slightly over 100 cases reported for tumor-to-tumor metastasis [2] . Meningiomas, which constitute approximately one-fifth of intracranial tumors, frequently act as hosts for metastases, [5] with breast and lung cancers being common primary tumors [ 7 ,8 ]. Additionally, metastatic foci originating from renal cell [9] , prostate [10] , and thyroid [11] carcinomas have been previously reported. Conversely, primary brain tumors such as meningioma, schwannoma, glioma, pituitary adenoma and craniopharyngioma, have been identified as components of intracranial collision tumors [ 1 ,2 ].

Intracranial metastasis from esophageal cancer is uncommon (0.3% to 13%) with reported median survival of less than a year [ 12 ,13 ]. A recent large database study of intracranial esophageal adenocarcinoma metastasis by Cheng S et al. [14] showed a positive association with brain metastasis occurrence with the following factors: younger age ( < 65 years), American Indian/Alaska Native race, lesions overlapping to different parts of esophagus than only upper third esophageal involvement, histologic subtype with higher nodal metastasis staging, and presence of liver metastatic foci. Our patient was 65 years of age at the time of presentation and already had liver metastatic foci showing poorly differentiated morphology on histopathology.

Campbell et al. proposed the following diagnostic criteria for tumor-to-tumor metastasis: presence of ≥2 primary tumors with the metastatic tumor establishing growth inside the host tumor which must be a true neoplasm [15] . Imaging characteristic seen with meningioma on MRI brain are isointense signal on T1WI, hypointense signal on T2WI, homogenous post contrast enhancement with a dural tail and buckling of underlying grey matter, were all present in our case, which helped to presume meningioma as a differential diagnosis on imaging. This was the only mass found in extra-axial location and was large in size, in contrast to other metastatic lesions which were intra-axial and much smaller in size. In addition, immunohistochemical analysis ( Fig. 4 ) showed the evidence of the growth of adenocarcinoma into meningioma, therefore satisfying the diagnostic criteria for tumor-to-tumor metastasis. Alternate noninfectious etiologies for rapid growth and quicker onset of neurological symptoms should include high-grade glioma such as glioblastoma multiforme and metastatic disease [16] . Accurate identification of tumor types offers significant clinical and management implications by influencing their surgical approach and postoperative care. Pathobiological expression of simultaneous growth of 2 tumors is complex and distinct from usual intracranial metastasis. Meningiomas, being the most common highly vascular intracranial tumor, often involved as host for additional metastatic neoplasm or as component of collision tumors [17] . Several factors have been implicated for this phenomenon including the role of hormone (progesterone and estrogen) receptors, cell-to-cell adhesion molecules, and a favorable metabolic and immunologic tumor micro-environment [ 18 ,19 ]. Better understanding of these interactions may offer additional therapeutic targets for the management of these patients.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: Our study sheds light on the infrequent presentation of esophageal adenocarcinoma metastasis into meningioma. Clinicians should be vigilant, considering tumor-to-tumor metastasis and collision tumors as important differentials in rapidly growing intracranial lesions associated with systemic solid organ malignancies. A comprehensive approach, combining imaging, and histology, is imperative for accurate diagnosis and optimal management.

div.p: Written informed consent for the publication of this case report was obtained from the patient.

figure.head: A
figure.figDesc: Fig. 1 -CT brain without contrast of 65-year-old patient presented with altered mental status. (A) Axial soft issue image of CT brain shows large mass in the left temporal lobe with effacement of left lateral ventricle and right sided midline shift. (B) Axial bone window of CT brain at the same level revelas no hyperostosis of adjacent bone or any calvarial metastasis.

figure.head: Fig. 2 -
figure.figDesc: Fig. 2 -MRI brain with and without contrast of 65-year-old patient presented with altered mental status. (A) Axial pre contrast T1W image shows the isointense large mass at left fronto-temporal convexity. (B) Axial T2W image shows hypointense mass with mild perilesional edema. (C) Axial post contrast T1W image shows large enhancing dural based extra-axial mass at left fronto-temporal convexity with right-sided midline shift.

figure.head: Fig. 3 -
figure.figDesc: Fig. 3 -MRI brain with and without contrast of 65-year-old patient presented with altered mental status. Axial postcontrast T1W image shows additional small enhancing lesions (arrows) in the supratentorial brain parenchyma.

figure.head: Fig. 4 -
figure.figDesc: Fig. 4 -Microscopic images of meningioma and metastatic adenocarcinoma. (A) Metastatic adenocarcinoma (left side, blue arrow) growing into meningioma (right side, yellow arrow). (B) The meningioma is positive for SSTR2A immunohistochemical stain; in contrast, the adenocarcinoma is negative. (C) The adenocarcinoma is positive for CK20, in contrast, the meningioma is negative. (D) CDX2 immunohistochemical stain is positive on adenocarcinoma but negative in meningioma.
